en: The Illustrated Exposition of the Correct [Usage of] the Three Robes, composed by the Śramaṇa Miaosheng of Kuaiji.
Regarding this Illustrated Exposition of the Correct [Usage of] the Three Robes: since the preceding work was written as a "Discernment of Errors," I have now further produced this illustration.

This is to clarify what is correct. Although the "Discerning Errors to Clarify the Correct" and the present work differ in their chronological order, they both aim to remedy the same defect regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Someone might say: "You previously argued that the diagrams produced by them were incorrect; why then do you now produce your own diagram?
Is this not an attempt to suppress others while exalting yourself, seeking victory and delighting in disputation? I reply: This is the reason for my current diagram.

Since the phenomena described in the Vinaya commentaries are difficult to comprehend, I have drawn diagrams to clarify the meanings of those annotations, so that the practical affairs of daily life may not remain obscure to people of this age; who then would say otherwise?

Yet, because people today cling to their own biased views as if they were self-attained realizations, there are erroneous "Diagrams of the Six Objects" (Ṣaḍvastu-cakra) circulating in the world—how could this be?

It is specifically because that [text] produced the diagrams; for their production was of no benefit and insufficient to supplement actual practice, serving only to misrepresent virtue and delude the people of the age—what else could this be but an error?
During my leisure time spent in study and reflection, I observed the inaccuracies within those diagrams;
therefore, I have composed the "Treatise on the Six Categories to Discern Errors," truly desiring to remedy this incipient malpractice.
Is it that I have intentionally created this present work? It is simply because the corrupt customs of those [others] have not yet been checked;

thus, having no other recourse, I have again produced this composition. It is not out of a desire for victory or a love of disputation, but rather because I wish to strike away their errors and lead them back to the correct path.
Regarding the illustrations and texts to be explained—whether extensive or concise—one first seeks their meaning according to the sequence of the diagrams and condenses them into fifteen sections.
Thereafter, one provides an explanation for each section following the diagrams; the meanings must be arranged in order to serve as a basis for the subsequent arising and maintenance of the robes.
1. First, the demonstration of the dimensions of the cloth and its colors; 2. The two lengths and shortnesses of the strips representing the Dharma;
3. Sewing one side with needle-stitches and the other with a plain seam; 4. The "leaf-pressing" and "bird-foot" seams; 5.
The leaves of the strips being uneven on the left and right; 6. Folding the four corners to provide assistance.
1. The sevenfold border should be placed around the edge; 2. the eight joints and corners should be adorned with *śrīvatsa* symbols;
3. it is clearly explained that the three seams form the border; 4. it is made double-layered and stitched with *maṇḍala* patterns;
5. hooks and loops are attached to the front and back; 6. there is an upper fold for wiping away grime and grease.
13. Distinguishing the places for folding, hooking, and tying; 14. Assembling and interpreting the text;
15. Drawing diagrams based on the measurements of the forearms.
These first twelve sections are intended to establish the sequence of the text so that people of the world may observe the diagrams and read the text.

The procedures for making robes are not established in vain; rather, they are designed to demonstrate that among the requirements for robe materials, the measurement of color and quantity takes precedence.

This is because all methods for making robes depend upon and rely upon the material substance, which must first be produced in accordance with the Dharma. Subsequently, the three types of dyed colors and the dimensions relative to the body’s length follow in sequence.
Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the nature of the material first, after which the dyeing and discoloration may proceed as prescribed.
According to the Dharma-measure of the cubit (*hasta*), when one intends to cut and sew [the cloth], one must distinguish its length and breadth.
Thus, the long and short strips manifest the sequence of the Dharma.
Once the length and breadth are evident, one must first stitch across one side of each strip horizontally to form the appearance of petals; having thus stitched across one side, one then opens it.
As for one side, it should be sewn with a "bird's foot" stitch (*sakuji-sei*) and pressed down; therefore, after pressing the leaves with the bird's foot stitch, four [stitches] arise.
Having finished the cross-stitching along the strips, one should join all the strips and press them together in sequence. This is like the method of cross-stitching the horizontal leaves;
because they are stitched vertically, the strip-leaves do not lean to the left or right. Fifth, the strip-leaves are stitched in accordance with the direction of the growth.
Once this has been done, one uses the auxiliary threads to mark the four corners according to the text and folds them;

thus, after the auxiliary threads have marked the four corners, the sixth step produces the garment’s form. Fearing that the four sides might quickly deteriorate, one then secures a border around the perimeter;
this is the seventh step. Once the border has been secured according to the rules, one should follow the traditional text to embroider the *wan* character upon it.

1. The corner-knots (jiejiao) and the *svastika* (wanzizi) are produced; 2. next, eight [stitches] arise, and upon their completion, the surrounding border (sizhouyuan) is still feared not yet firm, so one should follow other sections to break the border and sew it;
thus, 3. three stitches for breaking the border arise; 4. next, nine arise, and the leaf-patterned border (*tiaoye bianyuan*) is completed;
as this was previously a single-layer work, one must perform a double-layered *man* (gauze-like) stitch; thus, 5. ten arise, and the pins (*zhan*) are formed.
Once the lacing is finished, when it comes to putting on the garment, hooks and loops must necessarily be used; therefore, hooks and loops are attached at the front and back.

Next is the eleventh [section], which arises from the need for pulling when donning the garment. Since this area is prone to collecting much oil and grime, and one anticipates frequent washing, the twelfth section arises from the consideration of where the dirt and grease will accumulate.
These twelve sections, in their sequential order of arising, constitute the systematic arrangement for making the robe. There is no other.
This is an error. If the two lower robes are made as single-layered garments, then the tenth layer is excluded;
they consist merely of eleven sections. As for the remaining three sections of the text, their placement—whether before or after—is irrelevant;
this was simply recorded for convenience to distinguish the meaning of whether such errors exist or not.

The *saṃghāṭī* (this is a Sanskrit term; translated according to its function as "the robe for entering royal palaces and villages")—The Ritual for Receiving the Robe (one should request a person to act as the witness for the *karmavācanā*, saying:
[as follows]). This ritual for relinquishing and receiving [the robe] should appear below the diagram of the *kāṣāya*.

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], accept this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips, measuring [number] spans in length and [number] spans in width, a robe made of cut and sewn patches. (Recite three times)."
The Procedure for Renouncing the Robe:
"Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe was previously accepted as one of my three robes;
I now renounce it. (Recite once.)
Regarding the seven- and five-striped robes, one simply changes "saṃghāṭī" to "uttarāsaṅga" and "antarvāsaka"; the rest of the phrasing is the same as above.
In this diagram, the style is based on the lowest grade of the nine grades of the *saṃghāṭī*; as for the eleven- and thirteen-striped robes...
Those with nine strips, all of which are two long and one short, belong to the lower grade (this category is the lower grade).
Those with fifteen, seventeen, or nineteen strips, all of which are three long and one short, are called the middle grade.
Those with twenty-one, twenty-three, or twenty-five strips, all of which are four long and one short, belong to the upper grade. The above nine grades are all *saṃghāṭī* robes.
Uttarāsaṅga (translated as "garment for entering the assembly" based on its usage):
The ritual for adding the seven-strip [robe].
Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this seven-strip uttarāsaṅga robe for two [uses].
[The robe] one *cubit* long and [the other] short (cut and folded leaves), to be worn (three recitations).
*Antarvāsa* (translated as "garment for walking in the courtyard or for miscellaneous tasks"),
with the addition of the five-fold method (same as above).

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], receive this five-panel *antarvāsa* robe—cut, folded, and layered—with one length and one short side (measuring one *vitasti* long and one *vitasti* wide). I shall maintain it. (Recite three times.)

This illustration of the robe’s form is based on the nine-strip *saṃghāṭī* of the lower grade; however, when actually making the robe, one may produce it according to one’s preference in any of the nine grades, depending on the amount of cloth material available.
Since the regulations for this *saṃghāṭī* are now clear, the seven-strip and five-strip robes may be made by consulting the illustrations.

As for the procurement of materials, dyeing, folding the strips (*pattā*), gathering the strips (*saṃvartana*), and sewing them together (*mañca-karaṇa*), and so forth— [The text continues with detailed instructions on these processes.]
The details regarding the primary and secondary categories of robes, their measurements, and the requisite protective practices are as found in the commentaries and sub-commentaries;
they are all omitted here because my purpose is merely to clarify the method for cutting and sewing robes in order to remedy the prevalent abuses of the present age.
First, regarding the demonstration of the quantity of robes, wealth, and color:

the three robes must be made of cloth; they are to be sought through begging in accordance with the Dharma; and they must be dyed in one of the three types of "ruined colors" (kasāya). Those who know these matters in detail [should consult] the *Shuchao*, the *Shu*, and the section on the meaning of vestments (*zhangfu-yi*).
First, one calculates the robe materials by measuring the length of the body and its girth—whether lean or stout—such as five cubits in length and three cubits in width, or six [cubits].
Whether it be three cubits, three and a half cubits, or even according to the extreme size of one’s own body, one should adopt the standard measurement;
it is not necessary to rely strictly on the cubit, provided that one does not exceed the proper proportions. Wear it comfortably and conveniently (as detailed in the *Xianzheng yi*).

In the diagram representing the Dharma through long and short bars, the long bars symbolize the increase of the sages, while the short bars symbolize the decrease of ordinary beings. Thus, the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vṛtti) states:
"The sages increase while ordinary beings decrease; this is metaphorically represented by the abundance of the long and the scarcity of the short."
Regarding the diagram of the three-fold stitching on one side with a plain seam (*mān-sew*):
the single plain seam stitched on one side is intended to manifest the characteristics of the three robes (*tricīvara*).

Because they are plain-seamed internally while opening outward, the Patriarch who established the tradition of plain-seaming said, "Stitching on one side is precisely this. Furthermore, the reason one cannot simply sew straight is that [the fabric] must be folded back.
Regarding "stitching," it is because the clothing of worldly people is characterized by many seams and few stitches that this is considered a mark of heterodoxy;
therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü) is cited as stating that "avoiding stitching" is what the Buddha permitted for lawful possession and use.

One must use straight seams and not [imitate] the clothing of worldly people to distinguish oneself from heterodox customs, and furthermore, to prevent non-Buddhists [from using this as a pretext to extract the threads]. (This refers to preventing non-Buddhists from using it as an occasion to pull out the threads.)
Regarding the "bird's-foot stitch" for sewing the edges of petals in the diagram:
the bird's-foot stitch refers to the seam along the edge of the petals (as previously described in the reverse-stitch). One should join the petals at a T-shape;
once one side has been opened, perform the bird's-foot stitch at intervals of three or four inches to press them firmly together (according to the *Zhǔnchāo*).

One may also perform the "horse-tooth" stitch (*aśvadaṃṣṭrā*). Therefore, the *Karmavācanā-ṭīkā* states: "It is permitted to perform the 'bird-foot' stitch (*pakṣipāda-sevana*). The commentary explains: "The 'pressed leaf' (*nigṛhīta-patra*) stitch has a three-pronged appearance;

based on this, the horizontal and vertical leaf-patterns do not necessarily have to be fully opened. Furthermore, some rely on the *Vinayavibhaṅga-vyākhyā* (鈔), which quotes the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:

"If one sews leaves onto a robe, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for everything [beyond the prescribed limit]. Moreover, according to the note within the section on the formal ritual procedure (*vidhi*), if...
When folding the leaves so that the outer edges match, one might think it improper to stitch along one side while leaving the other open;
however, this passage concerning the "five parts" and so forth merely clarifies that one must not use a loose seam (*maṇḍala-sevana*), and does not mean that no stitching at all should be performed.
If one were to stubbornly adhere to the text regarding "leaving one side open," then even the measurements of three *hasta* for the width and so forth would become impossible to stitch.
If that is so, there is a tradition [in the scriptures] regarding the analogy of inserting a blade into the midst of leaves; now that the leaves are fully open, where is the blade hidden?
Furthermore, regarding the "seam of the bird's foot" mentioned in the commentary that presses down upon the leaves, where does it pierce?

Moreover, when the broad central leaves are spread apart, the wind may turn them over, and their mutual adherence is not always constant. Thus, we know that one cannot adhere to a single fixed interpretation.
The patterns are ornate, while the rest of the design is blocked out.
On five strips of leafy scrollwork, there are figures on the left and right;

within the central nine panels are these leaf-strips and birds. The feet of the birds are joined by seams, and these leaf-strips extend along the left edge. On the left side, four strips of leafy scrollwork follow the contour of the left edge.

(This refers to the fact that on the left side, the outermost strip is placed at the bottom, and the second, third, and fourth strips are layered in sequence to form the appearance of leaves. The *Chao* states: "The leaves are extremely broad, reaching four finger-widths, and extremely narrow, like a grain of barley;

these are all characteristics of the leaves. On the right side, there are four strips; the leaves follow the right side (the formation of the leaf-appearance by layering them in sequence may be understood by analogy with the above).
The single central strip is situated at the very top, covering both sides so that the leaf-appearance conforms to the left and right edges. Therefore, the *Chao* says: "On the left side..."

The left side slants toward the right, and the right side slants toward the central band; both sides slant in this manner, which signifies "following" (*mi*). (Its loose stitching and the binding of the leaf-patterns are identical to those of the *jiao-ye* [ornamental leaf] design.
In the diagram, the inner slanting stitches along the edges of the leaves originally formed a continuous perimeter, but this was altered when the garment was cut and tailored.
Because these stitches were executed on the inside of the garment, their pattern cannot be clearly seen in the diagram. (This principle is as follows:)
This is to cite and clarify it through the *Gantong zhuan* [Account of Spiritual Resonance].

Regarding the "diagram for pasting on the four corners to provide auxiliary support," those who fold the four corners do so solely for the purpose of providing auxiliary support to prevent rapid deterioration; there is no other significance. Therefore, regarding karma...
The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "It is for the purpose of counting, smoothing, holding up, and assisting with strength.
Regarding the four sides being provided with borders (*yuan*), the *Tu* (Diagram) shows borders placed on all four sides;
this is because the borders provide support so that [the object] does not quickly deteriorate. The *Chao* (Sub-commentary) says: "Permanently above and below..."
On the broken [patches], one should install borders that must necessarily include "thorns" (stitches) and so forth.

Regarding the eight joints, the corner thorns, and the *svastika* (卍): if one follows the meaning of the monastic robes (*cīvara*), it is criticized as saying "the Buddha’s chest has the ten-thousand-character design," with these applied in regular lines and so on. This is discarded by the transmitted texts;
furthermore, it seems to refer to the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), as it subsequently states, "on the left, the *niṣīdana*," and so forth.

The fact that the four corners of the robe and the heads of its long and short strips and seams are all embroidered with the *svastika* symbol follows the format of the five articles in the *Nanshan Bielü Linggan Zhuan* (Record of Miraculous Responses from the Separate Record of Mount Nanshan). Thus, that text states: "This is the robe of Krakucchanda Buddha...
[and so on] until after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, it was entrusted to the Dragon King Sāgara, who was instructed to fashion the eight [sections] according to this method."

Wanling continued to construct stupas as offerings to preserve the Dharma for posterity; on this *antarvāsaka*, the four corners and the seams are all marked with the *svastika* (the original text reads "wan") and other such symbols.
(The above is the main text. As for the seven-strip *saṃghāṭī*, the current practice is to wear it according to the rules (if one does not wear it, that is permissible;
for example, when folding the four corners of the sitting mat).
9. Clarifying the Breaking of Edges:

Regarding the diagram of the three-seam robe with edges broken throughout its perimeter, the single seam broken in the center follows the textual account in the *Gantong zhuan* (Tradition of Spiritual Resonance) concerning the sewing of the three robes after breaking their edges.

I shall now briefly cite the relevant passage from that tradition along with an annotated explanation; thus, that text states: [Insert text from Gantong Zhuan] ... [Annotated Explanation] ... Thus ends the passage.

It is said that when the three robes (*tricīvara*) have their borders torn, one should sew them by stitching across the middle of the two torn edges within the perimeter, thereby making them durable and preventing rapid deterioration;

this is quite consistent with the intent of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding the application of borders, though it is even more robust than the method prescribed in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Throughout the region south of the Yangtze River, everyone practices in this way, so why do you not do so?

I replied: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* contains no such text, therefore the three seams are omitted. [The Master] raised the point that our own school has no such text, yet he answered that since the four-sided border originally has two seams and the torn border has one seam, there are thus three seams in total; now, as for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*...

It simply says that when one prepares the border (*pratisaṃdhi*), there are two seams; therefore it is said that "the three seams are severed. Alternatively, this may correspond to the previous question which asked about sewing the torn borders of the three robes (*tricīvara*); since those four characters—"robe," "torn," "border," and "sew"—are omitted in the current answer, it merely says "three seams.

This is likely for the sake of brevity in the redaction, as the question was broad while the answer is concise. Answer: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* contains the text; how can you not employ this regulation? There are reasons why it must be practiced.
(The text of the deity’s second response is clear enough, yet I have not yet found the text in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. If I later find a text that differs from this, I shall certainly follow it.)

In the diagram illustrating the ten methods of making *mañca-stitching*, the stitching that runs around the perimeter within the *mañca-stitching* refers to the seams for constructing a double-layered *saṃghāṭī*.
These must not be intermingled with the internal leaf-like seams; therefore, one should stitch them after the grain has been removed. This is all based on the standard rule.
In the *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance), a celestial deity revealed to [Daoxuan] the method for re-making the *saṃghāṭī* robe at Mount Nanshan.

I have here fully cited the text of the *zhuan*, providing a brief explanation according to the difficulties encountered, so that those newly entering the study may not fall into error regarding the transmission.

This differs from others who cite the *zhuan* text alone, as they all share the same flavor [of misunderstanding]. The *zhuan* states: "Furthermore, the *saṃghāṭī* was re-made by the Master; his contemporaries followed this practice. However, during the former era..."
Regarding the statement that there are three layers beneath [the outer robe], how could this be so? According to the Buddha’s regulations, a newly made *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) consists of two layers;

the deities of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan) maintain that one should follow this practice. However, when it is made as a single layer, it is subsequently joined by sandwiching it between widths of cloth.

Furthermore, if it is not made of cut-and-sewn patches (*khaṇḍa*), then even when the inner layer is made as a single piece, it inherently possesses two layers, which are further augmented by the joining of the cloth widths.
Because one layer is sandwiched between two others, the leaf-patterns appear to run from top to bottom; thus, there are three layers.
The celestial deity said, "The strips and leaves must both have two layers, yet since the interior of the leaf already has three layers, how could this be so?

He then asked about its construction (this was the Great Master’s question). [The deity] immediately grasped my robe to demonstrate it (the deity’s demonstration). This leaf-pattern represents a rice paddy field.

Regarding the ridges and boundaries of fields: in the cultivation of paddy fields, whether high or low, there must necessarily be ridges and boundaries. Now, the Dharma-robes are the "fields of merit" (*kṣetra*).
Since the leaves [of the robes] vary in length and the upper and lower parts differ, they are patterned accordingly to represent this.
After the wheat has been harvested, one wishes to explain this meaning; first, let us provide a critical assessment: "In accordance with... [End of fragment].

The commentary states: "The phrase 'the text applies to both the inner and outer' means that, at first glance, the textual flow suggests sewing [patches] on the inside of the field-like boundaries outside the robe;
thus, one would first indicate the boundaries and only then state that one uses cut-and-sewn cloth segments to sew on the inside.
However, as there is no textual authority for this, one may instead follow the *Nanshan* [Vinaya] tradition to re-make the *kaṣāya* (great robe), using cloth throughout the interior of the garment.

Regarding the *maṇḍala* (patch) and the celestial deity (*devatā*), the refutation does not merely state two points—that it is not a single piece nor is it cut into sections—and further, it does not mention the fault of being multi-layered as being "inappropriate for the inner lining of the robe.
This may be taken as a precedent for the fact that the *Nanshan* [Zongjing] was not originally a pattern for the *saṃghāṭī*.
It also accords with the underlying intent of the refutation by the celestial deity; thus, the phrase "inner lining" (*lixiang*) in the text appears to have a basis in the scriptural wording.
Next, regarding the "elimination of the text" (*xiāowén*): this refers to the fact that within each leaf and between each rib there is one layer [of cloth].
One should separately apply pieces of cut-and-sewn cloth (*katicīvara*) according to the length and width of the ribs; these are sewn to join with the leaves inside the *saṃghāṭī*.
Furthermore, because it was troublesome for the needlework to coincide with the stitching of the leaves, it is further stated: "after removing the barley-grain [pattern]"; this means "removing."

After the grain has been removed, one pricks [the cloth] with a needle; some say that using a piece of cloth to remove the amount of the grain would leave single, sparse areas and fail to achieve two layers.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the Great Robe (saṃghāṭī) made by the masters of the Southern Mountain had three layers, when investigating the intent behind the rule for making it double-layered, the *Śūtra* states:
"The heavy and thick robe covers the body; the Great Rite is thus complete according to the Holy Rule."
There is a reason for this: although the current multiple layers do not deviate from principle, they suffer from the flaw of being incomplete.

Even the celestial deities rebuked [the previous view], stating that what lies beneath the upper layer consists of three layers; yet it even goes so far as to say there are two, and furthermore, many more.

Now, within these specific provisions, you instead maintain that there is only a single layer, which is difficult to believe on principle. Moreover, since the regulation was originally for a single layer, it is still considered "heavy" (redundant) even when applied to a single layer.
It has never been the case that one who acts contrary to the established rules and considers such solitary deviation to be correct has ever succeeded.
Thus, within these regulations, the "seed-field" (*miao-tian*) and the "hereditary field" (*shi-tian*) are filled with the five grains, which is why they are called "fields.
Now, the "field of respect" (*jing-tian*) of the Dharma robes is likewise filled with segments of cloth inside the *saṃghāṭī*, which are sewn there; therefore, it also represents its "seed-field."
This does not mean that the other two robes, when made singly, cannot be called "fields" (*kṣetra*); it is merely that the characteristics of a field's crops are slightly deficient.

Furthermore, it is because the deities do not manifest [their presence] in those other two robes. Moreover, since the Great Robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is subject to the regulation of being made with multiple layers, it fully manifests [the presence of the deities].
It is also like how in the world, fields are called "fields" whether they grow in summer or harvest in autumn. Furthermore, [this is evident] in such instances as entering a village and so forth.

Regarding the characteristics of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*): the two lower robes (*antarvāsa* and *saṃkakṣikā*) are permitted to be worn singly when entering a village, as the Buddha’s regulations do not allow for being without clothing;

however, this is not what is being explained here. As for the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), because it possesses the full characteristics of the field of merit, the regulation states that it must be doubled.

Furthermore, although the great robe may be made as a single layer and can be formally received and maintained (*parigraha*), its use as a garment is not permitted because its characteristics as a field of merit are not yet complete; thus, it is regulated that it must be doubled.

It is only when [the robe] is made that one may receive and use it; the fact that the five- and seven-strip robes have slightly fewer seed-patches (*bīja-lakṣaṇa*) can be understood by this principle.

This is a symbolic representation of the Dharma (*dharma-pratibimba*); it is not necessarily the case that all three robes must symbolize [specific features]. However, fearing those who would cling to the literal text and become obstructed by words and forms, I have provided these detailed explanations.
Is it not likewise the case that the leaf-patterns represent the appearance of irrigation channels? For in the world, there are always animals kept outside the boundaries of the fields and ridges.

The irrigation channels of water within the present-day dharma-robe are represented by the inner seams and outer openings of the robe’s panels; the two side-seams on the left and right represent the ridges and boundaries of the fields.
Therefore, the opening in the middle of each panel represents the accumulation of water, which is the characteristic of a channel.

Alternatively, it may be said that the openings in the panels represent the characteristics of the channels, for just as there are elevations and depressions in worldly fields, so too are there upper and lower sections in the robe’s panels, and the fields must necessarily have openings.

The ridges serve as ditches; clothing must have its seams opened so that the inner layers may be seen, for when things are similar in their characteristics and categories, they can be represented by one another.

Just as ditches and channels must be used to drain water, and water necessarily flows from high to low, so too, when a field has water, one must open the boundaries of the ridges to form ditches and channels to drain that water, thereby ensuring that the superior sprouts grow at various elevations to nourish their forms.
It is ordained that this dharma-robe, as a field of respect (*kṣetra*), must manifest its features like the ridges and furrows of a field to resemble the drainage of water;

it must ensure that the characteristics of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) appear in varying heights so that they may give rise to wholesome use for the salvation of all beings. Thus, the Commentary states:
"Just as the rice fields of the world are distinguished by the high and low levels of the water, the robes worn by śramaṇas manifest in long and short lengths for the same reason."

The Dharma robes and the field of reverence are for the benefit of all; as for the words spoken above, one looks from the leaves toward the branches in successive order, and from the branches toward the leaves in successive order, thereby opening the leaves.
The □□ character is situated above the line; thus, it is said that the "leaf" represents the appearance of the channel.
Regarding the eleven [items] joined before and after with hooks and clasps:
the hooks and clasps before and after in the diagram are as shown in the illustrations, following the *Chao* and the *Shu* as well. According to the text, they merely extend horizontally.

Regarding the measurements of four or eight finger-widths for the vertical sides on the left and right, the absence of a fixed textual prescription for the hooks and ties is due to the fact that human body proportions are not fixed at a single size;
rather, they are adjusted according to the individual's own body. For the time being, this diagram follows the manner of wearing:
the left side covers the shoulder and arm, while the right corner wraps around the left arm, and is thus roughly divided.

Regarding its characteristics, when it comes to making robes, they do not necessarily conform to the diagrams; the drawings made by others merely mark out a number of strips and do not mention hooks and ties.
Therefore, the *Chao* (Excerpts) states that the Buddha himself instructed the bhikṣus on the method for applying leather straps and ties:

"Four finger-widths from the front edge, apply a leather strap (some call this a 'handle'—*xuan*—as in the handle of a cauldron); eight finger-widths from the back edge, apply the tie," and so forth. Thus, it is based on this.
I shall now clarify the errors of contemporary practitioners: they mistakenly attach the rear fastener (*nīvi*) on the middle fold and the front hook (*aṅkuśa*) on the right corner.
Consequently, when the three robes (*tricīvara*) are worn over the body, they only encircle the left arm and fail to cover the rest of the body.

Regarding the origins of the robe’s front and back (as detailed in the *Gantong zhuan*), both the draping over the shoulder and the draping over the arm originate from the right corner; today, these are suddenly discarded, and one simply uses the [front] edge directly.

To attach [the corner] to the right shoulder is an error resulting from a lack of reflection; furthermore, to place this short corner upon the shoulder again is based on the textual description of "draping over the shoulder," which is an extreme case of such lack of reflection.

Moreover, according to the *Chuanwen* (Explanatory Text), the beginning and end of the practice of draping the robe’s corner over the shoulder originally involved the construction of hooks and fasteners (*gou-niu*).
If one were to merely pull and drag this short corner [to that position], it would not accord with the original intent.
Since there were originally no hooks or ties upon the shoulder, the robe would fall as soon as one let go; how then could it be draped over the shoulder?
Upon examining the beginning and end of the robe’s corners, it was found that they possessed hooks and ties, as well as shoulder-weights, which enabled it to be draped over the shoulder.

This was because the right corner of the robe was long enough to be draped over the shoulder. Later, when it was blown away by the wind, people began to use the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) as a shoulder-weight.
Nowadays, people place short horns upon their shoulders; if there is a fastening, they remain secure, but if there is no fastening, they fall off.
This is truly unacceptable as a reason for not adopting the fastener, which was designed to prevent them from being blown away by the wind.

Furthermore, since the textual description of "shoulder-draping" (dajiān) appeared later, it superseded the earlier teaching (in the *Yeshu*, the description of "shoulder-draping" appears first, while the mention of "encircling the left arm" appears later). Moreover, the commentaries and transmissions belong to the specific compositions of individual schools.
How could one fail to understand the intent of the Sage and persist in the practices of both houses?

Moreover, that which was shown by the heavenly deity and heard directly from the Buddha has been reverently recorded in the Southern Mountains texts and inscribed in the biographies; it is truly possible to take the textual accounts of these later traditions as authoritative and no longer harbor doubts.
That we do not follow the textual accounts precisely now is merely due to the fact that the corner of the robe being worn is caught on a hook.
Since one already harbors doubts regarding the chest area and it is difficult to rectify past errors, one must rely on the *Shuchao* (Commentary), which states:

"The intention of 'placing it over the shoulder' is clearly evident. Furthermore, if one separately installs hooks and loops, whether there be one, two, or three layers of fabric, there is no standard and no authoritative teaching to rely upon;
for the *Shuchao* merely says to "fold the four corners" and does not mention separately installing loops.
Regarding this, there are many who claim that it has been transformed into a corrupt custom by a single individual, leading to extreme absurdities among the masses.
Consequently, there are those who, having not studied the teachings since birth and possessing no knowledge of them, inherit these corrupt customs and erroneously construct [the term] *kui* (袿).
They claim that the garment is intended to serve as a covering for the body. When questioned about the reason for this, they reply, "I follow the scriptural texts. How truly laughable!
That the corruption of customs and transformations has become so extreme as to reach such a state is truly lamentable.
Regarding the "Grease on the Shoulders" diagram,
the *Chao* (Excerpts) states that grease should be applied to the shoulder area, while the *Shu* (Commentary) states that it should be washed frequently.
Since this robe is feared to wear out quickly, it is sufficient for it to be pure even if only the worn parts are patched.

Thirteen: Regarding the folding and placement of hooks and loops, many people nowadays separately place small square patches at the locations of the hooks and loops when folding; however, no textual authority for this has been seen. If one follows [the standard rules]...
Regarding the folding of the four corners: those who assist by lifting and supporting [the robe] find that the hooks and fastenings (*gūnyu*) are most essential for being lifted.

Thus, even if one folds [the corners], there is no error in principle, as this too is an act of mutual assistance. However, for the heavy *saṃghāṭī*, when made with strips and leaves, it need only have two layers;
it is unnecessary to fold it [further]. (Folding it is likewise without fault. As for the seven- or five-strip robes, if the hooks and fastenings...

Regarding the leaves, there is no need to fold them; as for the fruit within the stalks, since they consist of only a single layer, one might worry that they would break too quickly when pulled by the hooks and ties.
Therefore, it is appropriate to fold them at the four corners as a precaution. In truth, there is no textual prohibition against this—what fault could there be?
Nowadays, there are those who fondly attack unconventional practices and recklessly disparage the needlework, claiming that what is called a "platform" (tánzǐ) is incorrect; such views are mistaken.

Not realizing that this small square piece has no markings to serve as a basis for folding or attaching a loop, and that since the body of the *tánzǐ* lacks the name "*tánzǐ*," why trouble yourself with such groundless denunciations? This is truly like adding a dream upon a dream.
The fourteenth assembly extracts and explains the text;

however, this [passage] regarding the re-making of the *saṃghāṭī* appears to be inconsistent with the *Śrīlāta-vinaya-śīla-saṃgraha* (the *Chao*), which extracts the text concerning the making of the *saṃghāṭī* and so forth.
In order to ensure that the citation from that [text] does not contradict this passage, I have briefly harmonized them.

Regarding the method of disassembling [the robes], the *Jiecao* (Excerpts) states: "If, among the two robes, one remains with a heavy number of layers—such as two, three, or four layers—one should disassemble it to make a *saṃghāṭī*, and so on down to an *antarvāsaka*.

Since it says 'disassemble to make,' this means that from within the strips of the robe, one removes a section of cloth and re-makes it; it does not mean that one must necessarily remove the entire garment."

Regarding the phrase "because it is a completed garment," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "It merely permits one to pluck apart the seams and leaves of the fabric to make a robe, etc.;

it does not say to pluck apart a garment that has already been fully completed. If worldly people should doubt this, wondering how much effort it would take to pluck down a section of cloth from a finished garment, please examine the text of the *Shu* carefully.

Because it is a garment made from old materials, this allowance is opened so that one may use such a piece of cloth to roughly complete the work quickly and temporarily fulfill the requirements for the color of the robe.
The *Ear-If-So* (Ri-nikao) further states: "Regarding 'picking out and carrying while traveling,' it does not say to 'make [it] again.
This is because the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is heavy; therefore, one is permitted to pick out individual sections from its strips and carry only a single garment while traveling.

What is valued is the lightness of what is carried and lifted, so there is no necessity to make [a new robe] again. Furthermore, this does not mean picking out a fully completed garment. If that were the case, then this..."
Re-making the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) when there is a specific occasion allows for its parts to be detached; this is not inconsistent with the text of the *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Fifteenth, regarding the diagram:
the measurements for the *saṃghāṭī* in the diagram are based on the maximum dimensions according to the Sarvāstivāda school, being six *hasta* in length and three and a half *hasta* in width.

(The dimensions were originally one *zhang* and eight *cun* in length and six feet and three *cun* in width. Now, the length is reduced by one foot and eight *fen* to correspond to the one *zhang* and eight *cun* of the middle [standard], and the width is reduced by six *cun* and three *fen* to correspond to the six feet and three *cun* of the middle [standard].

For the seven- and five-line [robes], they also follow the Sarvāstivāda standard of five *hasta* in length and three *hasta* in width (which is nine feet in length and five feet and four *cun* in width).

Now, the length is reduced by nine *cun* to correspond to the nine feet of the middle [standard], and the width is reduced by five *cun* and four *fen* to correspond to the five feet and four *cun* of the middle [standard]. Thus, both the width and the length are [adjusted] accordingly.

Regarding the reliance on measurements, the noble ones take the sacred teachings as the standard for drawing their diagrams. When it comes to actual practice, the length and width do not necessarily conform to the cubit-measurements of the diagram;
thus, the *Zhangfu yi* (Meaning of Robes) states that "three cubits or five cubits" is merely a general approximation.

In practice, one should adapt to the circumstances rather than being restricted by formal prescriptions. This differs from those who arbitrarily draw diagrams without standards for length and width, which leads to excessive breadth.

The inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) is generally longer, while the middle robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is shorter; it is not the case that the seven-strip robe is long while the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is short.

Both arise from the subjective mind of the master, so do not rely on painted diagrams. This work, though lacking merit, has already been prepared to rectify errors and describe the intermediate accounts.
On the first day of the early summer month in the sixteenth year of the Shaoxing era (the Bingyin year), his disciple Benhui re-opened the East Collection.
The Vinaya Master was the teacher of Dazhi Vinaya Master; he was Vinaya Master Huijian.
